finding.claim: DELETE /files/<fid> deletes any file without an authorization check, because the result of require_allowed (acl.is_allowed) is discarded and never aborts.
finding.source: Any HTTP client sending DELETE /files/<fid>; no credentials required. g.user may be None.

trace.note: Route accepts DELETE /files/<fid>; fid is attacker-chosen
load_user copies X-Session-User-Verified header into g.user without verification
f = STORE[fid] loads the target file
require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') called; return value not checked
is_allowed returns a boolean and never raises or aborts

finding.guards_checked: before_request only reads a header (views.py:10-12); no authentication decorator; is_allowed returns bool (acl.py:4-5) and the caller ignores it. rename_file's ensure_allowed does abort, so the defect is specific to this route.

verdict.guard_found: none. before_request (views.py:10-12) only copies a client-supplied header into g.user with no verification. delete_file (views.py:15-20) has no auth decorator. require_allowed is the alias for acl.is_allowed (views.py:4), which returns a bool and never aborts (acl.py:4-5). Its result is discarded as a bare statement at views.py:18, so del STORE[fid] at views.py:19 runs regardless. The abort-on-failure helper ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) is used only by rename_file (views.py:26), not by this route.
verdict.reason: The DELETE route at views.py:15-19 calls is_allowed via require_allowed at views.py:18 and discards its boolean return (acl.py:4-5 never aborts), so del STORE[fid] at views.py:19 executes for any caller, including one with no X-Session-User-Verified header (views.py:12). The attacker is anonymous, and the trace matches the code as written. The verdict assumes these two files are the whole application; I did not check for other middleware, since I could only read this directory.

finding.claim: User identity is taken from a client-supplied header with no verification, so any client can impersonate any user with grants, including write or delete holders.
finding.sink: Grant lookup grants.get(user) in acl.py:5, reached via views.py:18 (delete) and views.py:26 (rename)

trace.note: Value passed as user into the delete ACL check
Value passed as user into the write ACL check in rename_file
resource['grants'].get(user, []) keyed on the attacker-supplied value

finding.guards_checked: No signature, token, or session validation exists in this code. Trust is valid only if an upstream proxy sets or strips the header, and nothing in the repo shows that. Remains exploitable after F1 is fixed.

verdict.guard_found: No signature, token, or session check on the identity: views.py:12 copies the raw X-Session-User-Verified header into g.user with no validation. For rename, acl.py:8-10 ensure_allowed() aborts with 403 when is_allowed() is False, so the grant check at views.py:26 is effective, but it only checks whatever identity the header supplies. For delete, views.py:18 calls require_allowed (acl.py:4-5, an alias of is_allowed, which returns a bool) as a bare statement and discards the result, so no grant check gates delete at all.
verdict.reason: The header is copied unverified at views.py:12, and the only grant gate on the rename path, ensure_allowed at views.py:26 / acl.py:8-10, keys on that same header value, so any client that sets the header to a user holding write grants can rename files. The trace is accurate about the flow, but the delete path is worse than described: views.py:18 discards is_allowed's bool result, so delete is not gated by grants at all, and the candidate's "delete holder impersonation" framing understates it. The remaining uncertainty is whether an upstream proxy sets or strips this header, which the repo cannot show; absent that, the finding stands.

finding.claim: Unhandled KeyError on a missing file ID returns HTTP 500, while an existing but unauthorized file returns 403, so an attacker can enumerate valid file IDs.
finding.sink: STORE[fid] lookup raising KeyError (views.py:17 and views.py:25); 403 path at acl.py:10 via views.py:26

trace.note: f = STORE[fid] raises KeyError for unknown IDs, yielding 500
abort(403) for existing files lacking the grant

finding.guards_checked: No 404 handling or uniform error response exists. Low severity; reduced in impact if file IDs are unguessable.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only check on the lookup path is ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10), which runs only after STORE[fid] (views.py:25-26). There is no try/except around the lookup and no errorhandler in views.py, so a missing ID raises KeyError and Flask returns 500. The DELETE route (views.py:15-19) calls require_allowed (acl.py:4, a bool-returning is_allowed) as a bare statement at views.py:18 with its result discarded, so that route never returns 403 and deletes the entry regardless of grants.
verdict.reason: The lookup at views.py:17 and views.py:25 raises an unhandled KeyError (500) for unknown IDs, while the rename route reaches ensure_allowed and aborts 403 for existing files without the grant (acl.py:10, views.py:26). An anonymous attacker can send any X-Session-User-Verified header (views.py:12), so the 500-versus-403 differential enumerates valid IDs with no auth required; the candidate's trace is accurate for the rename route, but its "403 for existing files" framing does not hold for DELETE, which returns no 403 at all and is a separate, more serious defect (views.py:18 discards the is_allowed result). Severity stays low, since no ID-generation scheme in the code makes enumeration costly.
